title: Hydroxychloroquine Promotion — Trump Touts Unproven Drug Against FDA Warnings
description_short: Hydroxychloroquine Promotion — Trump Touts Unproven Drug Against FDA Warnings
description_medium: In March 2020, Donald Trump repeatedly promoted hydroxychloroquine as a possible COVID-19 treatment, calling it a “game changer” while medical officials were warning that evidence was limited and cardiac risks were possible. The FDA authorized emergency use that month, then revoked the authorization in June after studies found no benefit. Trump’s public advocacy coincided with rising demand and reported shortages for patients who relied on the drug for lupus.
description_long: Donald Trump began promoting hydroxychloroquine as a possible COVID-19 treatment in March 2020, describing it as a potential “game changer.” The drug had not been established as an effective treatment, and health officials warned about possible heart-related side effects. Trump also said he was taking it himself. In late March, the Food and Drug Administration authorized its emergency use for certain hospitalized patients when clinical trials were unavailable or participation was not feasible. The agency revoked that authorization in June after reviewing evidence that the drug was unlikely to be effective and could cause serious cardiac problems. During the period of public promotion, demand for hydroxychloroquine increased, and patients who used it for lupus reported difficulty obtaining prescriptions. The sequence placed presidential advocacy, uncertain medical evidence, and a federal authorization in the same rapidly changing public-health debate. The authorization’s later reversal made clear that the early permission did not establish the drug as a proven COVID-19 treatment.

title: Second Trump Assassination Attempt at Golf Course — Ryan Wesley Routh
description_short: Second Trump Assassination Attempt at Golf Course — Ryan Wesley Routh
description_medium: On September 15, 2024, a Secret Service agent protecting Donald Trump at his West Palm Beach golf course spotted a rifle pointed through the tree line. The armed suspect, Ryan Wesley Routh, fled before firing and was arrested nearby. Prosecutors later charged him with attempting to assassinate a presidential candidate. The incident renewed scrutiny of security around Trump during the final weeks of the campaign.
description_long: On September 15, 2024, Ryan Wesley Routh was found in the tree line alongside Donald Trump’s West Palm Beach golf course, where he had reportedly waited for about 12 hours with a semi-automatic rifle. A Secret Service agent spotted him, and Routh fled before firing. He was later arrested and charged with attempting to assassinate a presidential candidate. The incident came two months after a gunman wounded Trump at a campaign rally in Pennsylvania. Together, the two episodes raised urgent questions about the safety of a presidential candidate and the protection surrounding his campaign activities. Routh was described as a North Carolina construction worker and Ukraine war recruiter; reports also noted that he had posted online about wanting to kill Trump. Those details formed part of the investigation into the suspect, but they do not by themselves explain his motive. At the time of the reports, the assassination charge was an allegation and had not been tested at trial. The West Palm Beach incident ended with an arrest before Trump was harmed, while renewing attention to the risks of politically motivated violence during a divisive election campaign.

title: Trump 'Kamala Is for They/Them, I Am for You' — Systematic Transgender Attacks
description_short: Trump 'Kamala Is for They/Them, I Am for You' — Systematic Transgender Attacks
description_medium: Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign used the slogan “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” in television ads attacking Kamala Harris over transgender policy. The ads highlighted her past support for publicly funded gender-affirming care for incarcerated people, while using that narrow issue as a campaign contrast. CBS News reported the campaign spent $19 million airing the ads nearly 55,000 times from October 1 through 16, 2024.
description_long: During the 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump’s campaign made transgender policy a prominent attack line against Kamala Harris. Its television ad used the slogan “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” and featured Harris’s earlier support for publicly funded gender-affirming surgery for prisoners. The underlying position concerned care for incarcerated people; the ad presented it as a broader contrast between Harris and Trump. The message appeared in several versions and was heavily scheduled in battleground states, including during professional and college football broadcasts. A CBS News report cited by the linked article found that the campaign paid about $19 million to air the ad nearly 55,000 times between October 1 and October 16, 2024. The campaign’s repetition made transgender rights and health care a high-visibility election issue. The short slogan and frequent placement gave voters a simple contrast, while the specific policy at its center concerned a narrow question about care in prisons. The ad became one of the campaign’s most recognizable messages and kept that dispute in front of voters during the final weeks of the race.

title: Trump Promotes National Enquirer 'Cruz Sex Scandal' Story (2016)
description_short: Trump Promotes National Enquirer 'Cruz Sex Scandal' Story (2016)
description_medium: In March 2016, the National Enquirer published a front-page story alleging that Ted Cruz had affairs with five women. Donald Trump shared and publicly discussed the allegation during the Republican primary, while denying that he had any role in producing the story. Cruz accused Trump and his associates of planting it and called Trump a “sniveling coward.” The linked report records Cruz’s accusation; it does not establish that the campaign arranged the article.
description_long: The National Enquirer published a front-page article in March 2016 alleging that Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz had affairs with five women. Cruz denied the allegations and publicly blamed Donald Trump and people around him for the tabloid story. Trump amplified the article during the primary campaign, including on social media, while telling reporters he had nothing to do with it. He did not condemn the Enquirer for publishing the claim. Cruz called Trump a “sniveling coward” and accused his campaign of planting the story. He said the allegation was intended to damage him with voters and demanded that Trump answer for its publication. Trump denied responsibility. The dispute unfolded during a competitive Republican primary, when sensational personal claims could quickly become campaign talking points. What is documented is that an unverified allegation entered the contest, Trump helped circulate it, and Cruz accused his rival of using the tabloid to harm him. The article’s publication and Trump’s amplification are distinct from Cruz’s accusation about who was behind it; that accusation was not established by the report.

title: Tender Age Facilities — Babies and Toddlers Separated
description_short: Tender Age Facilities — Babies and Toddlers Separated
description_medium: In 2018, the Trump administration’s family-separation policy reached babies and toddlers, some only months old. Children were placed in “tender age” shelters after being separated from their parents. Shelter workers described infants crying and young children lacking comfort, while the American Academy of Pediatrics warned that separation threatened children’s development and called the practice child abuse. Later testimony also raised concerns about inappropriate touching in the facilities and children who remained separated despite reunification orders.
description_long: The Trump administration’s 2018 family-separation policy affected very young children as well as older minors. Babies and toddlers, including some only a few months old, were taken from their parents and housed in facilities officials described as “tender age” shelters. Workers at the shelters described infants crying inconsolably and toddlers receiving inadequate comfort and care. The American Academy of Pediatrics condemned the separations as harmful to children’s health and development and called the policy child abuse. Later testimony by an HHS whistleblower raised an additional concern: some children had been inappropriately touched by facility staff. Family separation was followed by court-ordered efforts to reunite children with their parents, Some children remained separated even after court orders called for reunification. These reports focused attention on the effects of separation during a formative stage of development and on the government’s duty to protect children in its custody. The allegations about staff conduct and the incomplete reunifications added questions about safeguards and accountability in the facilities. The episode showed how enforcement policy brought very young children into a system whose care and reunification processes faced serious criticism.

title: Mass Deportation Operations Begin on Day One of Second Term
description_short: Mass Deportation Operations Begin on Day One of Second Term
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, hours after taking office, Donald Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border and ordered a broad enforcement crackdown. His administration directed federal agencies to begin expanded immigration operations and assigned military personnel to assist at the border. The rapid shift unsettled immigrant communities, while civil-rights groups challenged the measures and raised due-process concerns about how arrests and removals would be carried out.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Donald Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border and issued directives for a sweeping immigration crackdown. The administration ordered federal agencies to begin expanded enforcement operations and announced military assistance for border security. The measures signaled an immediate change in federal immigration priorities and were accompanied by plans for a much larger deportation effort. The speed and scale of the announced operations prompted fear in immigrant communities, with people concerned about going to work, sending children to school, or seeking medical care. Civil-rights organizations challenged the operations and raised due-process concerns about the speed and manner of arrests and removals. The announcement established the administration’s stated direction, while the legal challenges focused on how that policy would be carried out. The first-day directives therefore marked both an operational push and the beginning of a dispute over the rights of people subject to enforcement. The national emergency declaration also expanded the role of federal agencies in border policy, making the first day a significant shift in the government’s approach to immigration.

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Deported Despite Court Protection Order
description_short: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Deported Despite Court Protection Order
description_medium: In March 2025, the Trump administration deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident from El Salvador, despite a court order barring his removal to that country. He was sent to El Salvador’s CECOT prison. A federal judge later ordered officials to facilitate his return, and on April 10 the Supreme Court upheld that instruction. The administration argued it could not retrieve him from Salvadoran custody, making the case a test of compliance with court orders.
description_long: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national living in Maryland, was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 and held at the CECOT prison. A prior court order had barred his removal to El Salvador because of the danger he faced there. The administration later acknowledged that his deportation had been an error, but said it could not bring him back once he was in Salvadoran custody. A federal judge ordered the government to facilitate his return. On April 10, the Supreme Court upheld that requirement, directing the administration to take steps to secure his release and return while leaving the lower court to clarify the practical details. The dispute put the administration’s immigration enforcement against a specific judicial protection and raised a direct question about whether officials would carry out a court’s order after a person had been sent abroad. Abrego Garcia’s case became a prominent test of the limits of executive power and the ability of federal courts to enforce their rulings. The government’s position that it could not secure his release sharpened the conflict between its control over immigration enforcement and the court’s instruction.
